answer.summary: Scrum helps when it prompts teams to discuss and break down work, learn quickly from customers, and inspect and adapt how they work. A team that already communicates and can deliver effectively may not need Scrum’s formal framework or meeting overhead.

sections.heading: Practices that make Scrum useful
sections.content: Melissa says teams thrive when they talk about the work, break it down, and clarify it so developers can get started and ask important questions. Scrum’s useful underlying aim is to ship in chunks and get customer feedback faster; her team at OpenSky eventually found two-week sprints too long and shipped weekly. Teams should also inspect and adapt: keep practices that serve them and drop those that do not, rather than following meetings or ceremonies dogmatically.

sections.heading: When a formal framework may not be needed
sections.content: A framework can help when a team is not already having the conversations needed to understand and coordinate the work, or when a larger company needs rigor at scale. But if a team already talks regularly, knows what to work on, and has a way of getting work to customers, it may not need Scrum, prescribed two-week sprints, or extensive meetings. Perri says small startups generally do not need much of that overhead; some SaaS companies use Scrum without being dogmatic about it.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately describes talking through and breaking down work so the team understands it and can ask questions, and explains that frameworks can help when those practices are missing. It also notes that teams already communicating and delivering effectively may not need Scrum or a prescribed sprint cadence. The cited context supports the additional points about customer feedback, adapting practices, and scale.
